title: Orienting a map with a compass
def: Orienting a map means turning it so north on the map points to north on the ground, after allowing for declination, so the map matches what you see.
look: the map's north arrow or meridian lines
the compass needle settled and away from metal
known features ahead lining up with the map
use: Lay the compass on the map, line its edge with a north-south line, and turn map and compass together until the needle points to north, adjusted for the declination printed on the map.
not: Do not orient the map next to a vehicle, rifle, or phone, which can pull the needle. Do not forget declination on an older map.
steps: Set the compass for the map's declination.
Lay the compass edge on a north-south line.
Turn the map until the needle lines up.
Check that real features match the map.

title: Declination: magnetic versus true north
def: Declination is the angle between where a compass needle points (magnetic north) and true north on the map; it differs by place and slowly changes over the years.
look: the declination diagram and year printed on the map
a compass with an adjustable declination setting
bearings that drift off by the same few degrees
use: Look up current declination for your area from NOAA, set it on your compass or add or subtract it, and note the year of the value you used.
not: Do not trust an old map's printed value without checking its year, and do not hard-code one number for a whole region.

title: True north, magnetic north, and grid north
def: True north points to the North Pole, magnetic north is where a compass needle points, and grid north follows the vertical grid lines printed on a map; the small angles between them matter over distance.
look: the three-arrow diagram in a topographic map's margin
grid lines (UTM) on the map
the compass needle
use: Use the map's diagram to convert between them, and be consistent: plot and follow bearings in the same north.
not: Do not mix a grid bearing from the map with a magnetic bearing from the compass without converting.

title: Taking and following a compass bearing
def: A bearing is the direction to a target measured in degrees clockwise from north; you take it from the map or a landmark, then walk it by sighting from object to object.
look: the direction-of-travel arrow on the compass
the needle boxed in the orienting arrow
a tree or rock on the line ahead
use: Set the bearing, hold the compass level in front of you, turn until the needle sits in the orienting arrow, pick a landmark on the line, walk to it, and repeat.
not: Do not walk with your eyes on the compass the whole way, and do not take bearings near metal or a running vehicle.
steps: Set the bearing on the compass.
Box the needle in the orienting arrow.
Pick a landmark on the line.
Repeat until you reach the target.

title: Contour lines and terrain features
def: Contour lines join points of equal elevation, so their shape and spacing show the land: close lines are steep, wide lines are gentle, and Vs pointing uphill mark streams and draws.
look: contour interval printed in the margin
closed rings for hilltops, with tick marks for depressions
Vs pointing uphill for valleys and draws, downhill for spurs and ridges
use: Match the five main shapes, hill, saddle, valley, ridge, and depression, to what you see, and use them to plan routes that avoid steep ground.
not: Do not read a tight cluster of lines as a trail; it is a steep slope or cliff.

title: Measuring distance and keeping a pace count
def: Distance on a map is measured against its scale bar, and on the ground you track it with a pace count: the number of your double steps in 100 meters on your normal stride.
look: the scale bar in the map margin
your own tested pace count
more paces uphill, in brush, snow, or the dark
use: Measure your pace count on a known 100 m course, count every second step while walking, and tie a knot or move a bead at each 100 m.
not: Do not use someone else's pace count, and do not forget to add paces for slopes and rough ground.

title: GPS and phone versus map and compass
also: do I need a compass if I have a phone
def: A GPS or phone gives a fast position but needs battery and sky view; a paper map and baseplate compass keep working when the screen dies or the signal drops.
look: battery below half on a long day
deep canyons, heavy cover, or cliffs blocking the fix
a printed map of the area in your pack
use: Carry a paper map and compass as backup, keep the phone warm and in power-saving mode, and check your position on the map at each landmark.
not: Do not head out with only a phone, and do not trust a position that jumps around in thick cover.

title: Lost? Stop, think, observe, plan
def: When you realize you are lost, the first job is to stop moving, calm down, and work from your last known point; staying put is usually safest if you cannot work it out.
look: the last place you were sure of
streams, ridges, or roads you crossed
how much daylight, water, and warmth you have
use: Sit down, breathe, look and listen, retrace on the map if you can, and if not, stay put, make yourself visible and heard, and prepare for the night.
not: Do not keep walking hoping it turns familiar, split up a group, or travel at night in rough country.
steps: Think back to your last known point.
Plan: retrace a sure route or stay and signal.
call: Call 911 if you have signal; a text can go through when a call will not.

title: Handrails, catching features, and aiming off
def: Terrain association uses long features to guide you: a handrail is something you walk alongside, a catching feature stops you if you overshoot, and aiming off means deliberately aiming to one side of a target on a line feature.
look: a stream, ridge, trail, or field edge running your way
a road, river, or lake beyond your target
a known side to turn toward when you hit the line
use: Pick a handrail toward your goal, note a catching feature past it, and when heading for a point on a stream or trail, aim a little to one side so you know which way to turn.
not: Do not assume a stream leads to help; it can lead into cliffs, swamps, or thick brush.

title: When a phone compass is unreliable
def: A phone's compass is a magnetic sensor that metal, magnets in cases, vehicles, and a skipped calibration can throw off by many degrees.
look: a magnetic phone case or mount
readings that swing when you move near a truck or rifle
a calibration prompt
use: Calibrate by moving the phone in a figure-eight away from metal, remove magnetic cases, and cross-check against a baseplate compass or the sun.
not: Do not trust a phone compass inside a vehicle or next to steel.

title: Stream crossings: when to go around
def: A stream is safe to cross only when it is shallow, slow, and has a clear landing; knee-deep fast water can knock an adult down.
look: water above the knee or moving faster than a walk
muddy, rising water after rain
rapids, logjams, or falls downstream
use: Scout for a wide, shallow, braided spot, unbuckle the pack's hip belt, face upstream with a stick or partner, and shuffle your feet.
not: Do not cross in flood, above a logjam or falls, or barefoot on sharp rock, and do not tie yourself into a rope across fast water.
